body_text: When Fire Technology Goes Quiet, Value Becomes Clear July 28, 2026 by Kate Nadolski For today’s fire departments, access to information is just as important as access to physical equipment. Responders rely on technology to deliver incident details, location data, building information, and other critical insights that help them make informed decisions on every call. Although the department’s contingency plans kept communications operational, firefighters suddenly found themselves without many of the digital tools they used every day. "We still had our radios, but crews got into the rig and didn’t have any of their information in front of them on the MDT," Hebbeln said. The outage lasted only a few hours, but it immediately highlighted how heavily responders depend on mission-critical information while heading to a call. CAD details, call notes, location information, building access points, and pre-plan data that had become second nature were suddenly unavailable, all due to the construction crew’s error. "We’ve gotten so used to just having the information," Hebbeln said. "When it doesn’t work, it becomes painfully obvious that we really rely on this stuff. It makes our job that much easier." The experience wasn’t about losing technology — It was a reminder of the role technology plays in helping crews respond efficiently and confidently. Shortly after the incident, the fiber was repaired, and all access to technology was restored. For the Davenport Fire Department, the fiber outage served as an unexpected reminder of something easy to overlook: when technology works consistently, firefighters can focus on the job in front of them rather than the tools behind it… Sometimes, it takes a brief disruption to fully appreciate the value of having critical information available when every second counts. title: Best Social Listening Tools for Beauty Brands (Counterfeit Losses Up 24x)
summary: Counterfeit K-beauty losses hit $15.1M in 2025, up 24x YoY. Compare 9 social listening tools on video AI, dupe-culture coverage, and beauty-specific fit.
body_text: The best social listening tools for beauty brands in 2026 are the ones built to catch conversation that happens on camera, not just in captions. Syncly Social leads for brands that need to catch untagged shade-match, dupe-comparison, and ingredient-reaction conversation inside GRWM and swatch videos. Meltwater has the strongest named beauty customer roster of any vendor researched (Shiseido, Yves Rocher, Bon Parfumeur). Talkwalker is a genuine standout with a dedicated Beauty & Personal Care solutions page backed by a real case study. Sprout Social offers a current, quantified beauty result (Care to Beauty, 2024) at an accessible price. The stakes are real: counterfeit losses tied to Korean beauty brands alone hit an estimated $15.1 million in 2025 — a 24-fold jump year over year — and Beauty & Personal Care is now the single largest category on US TikTok Shop, at 22.5% of GMV and climbing. Beauty conversation doesn't behave like conversation in other categories. A shade-match complaint isn't typed, it's shown against skin. A dupe comparison is a side-by-side swatch, not a hashtag. Whether an influencer disclosed a paid partnership often shows up only in tone, not text. Tools built to catch keywords and hashtags miss most of this by design. That gap matters more this year than last. Counterfeit product conversation around Korean beauty brands has exploded, dupe culture has gone from niche to mainstream consumer behavior, and TikTok Shop has made beauty its single biggest category — all while ingredient reformulations driven by new EU restrictions are generating real backlash in the comments. Here's what to look for in a social listening tool built for this vertical, and how nine of the leading options actually compare. Why beauty brands need a different kind of social listening Cosmetics and skincare sit under FDA authority via the 2022 Modernization of Cosmetics Regulation Act, which added mandatory-recall powers the agency has already used twice in the past year. Neutrogena (Kenvue) recalled 1,312 cases of its makeup-remover wipes in September 2025 after testing found bacterial contamination, and the FDA classified it a Class II recall weeks later (Source: TopClassActions, 2025 ). Six benzoyl-peroxide acne treatments were voluntarily recalled in March 2025 over elevated benzene levels (Source: Cosmetics & Toiletries, 2025 ). Separately, new EU restrictions on cyclic silicones are forcing brands to reformulate decades-old products in real time. Estée Lauder's Double Wear Foundation was reformulated in 2026 to remove cyclopentasiloxane, and the resulting texture change sparked visible frustration in beauty forums and social conversation over the product's changed finish (Source: VITA Daily, 2026 ). Armani, Moroccanoil, Revlon, YSL Beauty, CoverGirl, and NARS are all navigating the same reformulation pressure (Source: American Salon, 2026 ). A social listening tool can't test a formula or file a recall. What it can legitimately do is surface how much reformulation or safety conversation exists, and what it's actually saying — a visibility layer, not a compliance system. Shade-matching is the other structural difference. A 2026 survey of more than 4,300 US women found only 22% believe beauty brands are "genuinely inclusive," 61% of respondents with darker skin tones say they've abandoned a brand over a shade-lineup failure, and 90% said they'd want customized shade matching if it were available (Source: The Benchmarking Company, 2026 ). The most-cited example of this backlash going viral remains Youthforia's 2023 foundation launch, where a creator's shade comparison drew more than 12 million views (Source: NBC News, 2023 ) — dated, but still the reference point industry commentary returns to. The conversations caption-only tools miss in beauty Dupe culture has moved from niche to mainstream: 82% of Gen Z say they plan to buy less-expensive "dupes" this holiday season (Source: PwC Holiday Outlook 2025 ). Dupe-culture conversation is the social-video-native pattern where creators compare a cheaper product side-by-side against a name-brand original — swatch tests, wear tests, ingredient-list comparisons — and it's disproportionately visual, not typed. Olaplex is the clearest example of a brand engaging directly with it: the hashtag #OLAPLEXDUPE passed 30 million views by late 2023, and Olaplex responded with its own influencer-driven "OLADUPÉ" campaign (Source: The Industry.beauty, 2023 ). Counterfeiting is the sharper edge of the same coin. Counterfeit-product losses tied to South Korean beauty brands hit roughly 22 billion won — about $15.1 million — in 2025, a 24-fold increase over the prior year, with 99% of detected shipments originating in China (Source: The Korea Herald, 2025 ). Manyo and Sulwhasoo were the most-counterfeited brands, and a single late-2025 raid in Foshan, China seized 56,000 counterfeit items targeting Beauty of Joseon and SKIN1004. A social listening tool doesn't stop counterfeiting or enforce IP takedowns. What it legitimately offers is visibility into how much dupe and counterfeit conversation exists, which products are being compared, and how sentiment is shifting — awareness a brand can act on, not an enforcement mechanism. Influencer disclosure adds a third layer specific to beauty. The FTC's Endorsement Guides create real exposure around seeding programs — the most substantiated recent precedent involving a skincare-adjacent brand is the FTC's case against Teami, LLC, which resulted in a $15.2 million judgment (partially suspended to $1 million) and formal warning letters to ten celebrity influencers, including Cardi B, for inadequate disclosure (Source: Davis+Gilbert LLP, 2023 ). That case is dated, but the underlying guidance — that a platform's built-in "Paid Partnership" tag alone doesn't satisfy disclosure requirements — is current. A listening tool can't audit legal compliance, but it can surface which creators are discussing a product and whether disclosure language shows up in what's captured. All three pressures compound against a commercial backdrop that's growing fast: Beauty & Personal Care is now the largest category on US TikTok Shop by GMV share, at 22.5% and growing 48% year over year, with Korean skincare specifically up 78% quarter over quarter (Source: Dashboardly, 2026 ). The category's 6-10% return rate is driven primarily by shade mismatch — a direct, structural link back to the inclusivity problem above. How we evaluated these tools Every vendor below was assessed against a simple, honest standard — the same way we'd approach any competitor analysis : does it have real, named beauty-industry customer evidence, or does it just claim general applicability? The distribution genuinely surprised us. Talkwalker, which showed no durable evidence in Food & Beverage or Consumer Goods research, turns out to have real, named beauty proof. YouScan, whose "visual-first" positioning would seem tailor-made for beauty's swatch-heavy content, has none at all. Meltwater's beauty roster is the strongest of any vendor in this research: Shiseido (50+ luxury brands across 120 countries, consolidated from a dozen-plus fragmented tools), Yves Rocher (regional influencer discovery), and Bon Parfumeur (a full influencer shortlist delivered in under a week via agency Digital Business Lab) (Source: Meltwater — Shiseido ; Meltwater — Yves Rocher ). Pricing: no public list price; analyst estimates place median spend around $25,000/year, ranging from $6,000 to $150,000+ depending on tier (Source: Vendr, 2026 ). 3. Sprinklr's beauty evidence is real but aging: a 2020 L'Oréal partnership announcement (36 brands, no disclosed performance metrics) and a more detailed 2021-22 Shiseido Japan case study showing 244% year-over-year owned-media growth and 406% UGC growth (Source: Sprinklr — Shiseido Japan ). Pricing: enterprise-only since self-serve was discontinued in April 2026; contracts typically start around $50,000/year with a median near $129,000/year (Source: Chatarmin, 2026 ). 4. Talkwalker Best for: beauty brands that want speech-to-text and logo/OCR video recognition — genuinely relevant to beauty's packaging- and swatch-heavy content — without paying for a full social publishing suite. This is a standout, easy to overlook if you've only seen Talkwalker pitched as a general-purpose platform: it maintains a dedicated "Beauty & Personal Care" solutions page and a separately published Yves Rocher case study covering raw-materials, eco-design, and consumer-intelligence use cases — genuine, current beauty-specific proof, stronger than the food-and-beverage or consumer-goods evidence it shows elsewhere, where it has no comparable named customer. Pricing: core plans run $79 to $399 per user/month; social listening is a custom-quoted add-on, not included in any base tier (Source: Sprout Social, 2026 ). 6. Brandwatch Best for: beauty brands with an insights team that wants ongoing ingredient and category-trend tracking, backed by deep historical data reaching back to 2010. Brandwatch's skincare-ingredient research is real and specific — ceramide mentions up 46%, niacinamide up 33%, cica up 32% (Source: Brandwatch, Oct 2023 ) — but no named beauty customer surfaced in this research, and the article itself is dated. Brandwatch's own 2026 roadmap lists deeper video and image analysis as a forward-looking goal, not a shipped feature. Pricing: no public list price; comparable estimates place entry tiers around $800-2,000/month, scaling to custom enterprise quotes. 7. The notable finding here is negative: despite a "visual listening" pitch that seems purpose-built for beauty's swatch and shade content, YouScan's public client list names Danone, Coca-Cola, McDonald's, and several agencies — zero beauty or personal-care brands. Worth knowing before assuming visual-first automatically means beauty-fit. Pricing: custom quote. 8. Brand24 Best for: budget-conscious teams whose needs are genuinely text- and keyword-first — brand names, a few competitors, review sites, basic caption and hashtag tracking. Brand24's public case studies list Uber, Hostinger, and several B2B/tech names — no beauty, cosmetics, or personal-care brand appears. It has no audio transcription or on-screen visual detection at any tier. Pricing: $199-1,499+/month depending on tier (Source: Brand24, 2026 ). 9. title: VDPHL01 Meets Primary Endpoint in Women: Positive Phase 2 Results from Study ‘207’
summary: Veradermics, Incorporated (NYSE: MANE) has reported positive topline results from the female treatment arms of Study ‘207’, an open-label Phase 2
body_text: Veradermics, Incorporated (NYSE: MANE) has reported positive topline results from the female treatment arms of Study ‘207’ , an open-label Phase 2 trial of VDPHL01 — the company’s extended-release oral minoxidil tablet — in women with mild-to-moderate androgenetic alopecia. The trial met its primary endpoint. What the Study Showed In the female arms, once-daily oral VDPHL01 produced a statistically significant and clinically meaningful increase in nonvellus target area hair count at week 24, measured as change from baseline — the trial’s primary efficacy endpoint. These are the first controlled efficacy data for VDPHL01 in women; to date, pivotal results had been reported only in men, in the Phase 2/3 Study ‘302’. “These results reinforce our confidence in VDPHL01’s potential to become a foundational treatment for the millions of women living with androgenetic alopecia.” Reid Waldman, M.D., Chief Executive Officer, Veradermics Investor Conference Call Veradermics is hosting an investor call and live webcast to review the results. Date Wednesday, July 15, 2026 Time 8:00 a.m. ET Format Investor call and live webcast, with accompanying slides Access Events page, Investors section of the Veradermics website Replay Available following the call About VDPHL01 VDPHL01 is an investigational, non-hormonal oral treatment in Phase 3 development for pattern hair loss in women and men. Its extended-release formulation is designed to deliver minoxidil with a more consistent exposure profile, avoiding the peak concentrations associated with the dose-limiting cardiovascular effects of conventional oral minoxidil. The company reports the earliest expiring patent term as 2043. Sources: FemTech Insider ; Veradermics via Business Wire (July 14, 2026).

title: Marketing The Anatomy of a Fake Invoice (And How to Stop One) Invoice fraud cost businesses billions last year, and it rarely looks like an attack. Here's how a fake invoice works, and how structured invoicing stops it.
body_text: ‍ Trust, Betrayed: The Anatomy of a Fake Invoice In 2025, businesses reported losing more than 3 billion dollars to a single kind of fraud. Almost none of it involved breaking in. It arrived as an invoice. That is the figure the FBI puts on business email compromise for the year: just over 3 billion dollars, and business email compromise is, at its heart, fake-invoice and vendor-impersonation fraud. It is the second most costly category of cybercrime in the United States, and it almost never looks like crime. There is no broken door. There is a familiar vendor, an expected amount, and one detail quietly changed. If money is trust in motion, then a fake invoice is the moment someone hijacks the motion. It is trust, betrayed. How the Betrayal Works Picture the most ordinary thing in your week. An invoice arrives from a supplier you already pay. The logo is right. The amount is roughly what you expected. The email reads exactly like the last one. The only difference, buried in the payment details, is the account number. That is the entire attack. Not a sophisticated hack, but a familiar relationship, impersonated. Sometimes the criminal clones a vendor's domain, swapping one character no one reads closely. Sometimes they get into the supplier's real email account, so the message passes every security check because it genuinely came from there. Then comes the line that does the damage: a quiet note that the bank details have changed, please update your records. It works because we have been trained to trust the routine. Nobody re-verifies the invoice they have paid fifty times. As the people who study this fraud put it, these are legitimate-looking payments, and that is exactly what makes them so hard to catch. It looks exactly like the last invoice you paid. That resemblance is the weapon. Why Manual Invoicing Leaves the Door Open Here is the uncomfortable part. The reason this fraud succeeds so often is not that criminals are brilliant. It is that most invoicing is built on email and PDFs, and email and PDFs were never built for trust. A PDF can be edited. An email address can be faked. A bank-detail change can be accepted by a single person, informally, with nothing logging who changed what or when. There is no validated record of who your vendor really is, and no audit trail to reconstruct afterward. So the altered invoice looks like every other attachment in the inbox, right up until the money is gone. The same gap creates quieter losses too. By SAP Concur's own measure , the typical business sees a duplicate invoice rate of around 1.3 percent, with each duplicate worth roughly 2,000 dollars. That is not even a criminal. That is just a process with no structure, leaking money in the background. Why This Hits Africa Hard The exposure is sharpest where money is moving fastest. Across Africa, digital payments have scaled at extraordinary speed, often faster than the controls meant to protect them. Interpol now flags business email compromise as one of the continent's most significant and growing cyber threats, and names Nigeria among its main hubs, with cybercrime losses across Africa estimated in the billions over recent years. This is also exactly why Nigeria's move to mandate structured, government-validated e-invoicing matters. A validated invoice with a unique reference number is far harder to fake than a PDF in an inbox. The defense is becoming the law. You do not beat invoice fraud by being more careful with email. You beat it by taking email out of the path. How You Actually Stop It The fix is not vigilance. Vigilance fails, because the whole point of the fraud is that it looks normal. The fix is structure. When vendor records are locked and validated, a bank-detail change cannot be made by an inbound email. It takes an authenticated, logged action. When approvals are mandatory, no single person can both create and pay. When invoices are structured data with unique reference numbers, a duplicate becomes impossible to pay twice and an altered invoice stands out against the original. And when every action leaves an audit trail, the anomaly surfaces in real time, not at month-end when the money has already moved. That is what settlement-native infrastructure does. It closes the loop between the invoice and the payment, and shrinks the space where a hijacked detail can slip through. The Takeaway Invoice fraud is not really a technology problem. It is a trust problem. It works by wearing the face of a relationship you already have, and changing one thing you were never going to check. You cannot out-careful it. But you can make trust verifiable, so that an invoice has to prove it is what it claims to be before a single naira moves. That is the difference between hoping your team catches the fake one, and building a system where the fake one cannot get through. Ready to make every invoice prove itself before you pay? Joy offers hundreds of free digital and premium paper save the date designs you can filter by style, color, format, and more. Browse all save the date designs on Joy . What Is a Save the Date? A save the date is the first formal communication your guests receive about your wedding. It is not the invitation — it is the advance notice that tells people your names, wedding date, and general location so they can block the date on their calendars, request time off work, and start planning travel. Save the dates go out before formal invitations and typically include: Both partners’ names The wedding date The city or venue location (full address is not required yet) A note that a formal invitation will follow Your wedding website URL (so guests can find details as you add them) Save the dates come in many formats: printed cards, magnets, postcards, digital designs sent via email or text, and even creative options like bottle openers or custom illustrations. The format you choose sets the tone for your entire wedding — a foil-pressed card signals a formal celebration, while a playful digital design suggests a more relaxed affair. When Should You Send Save the Dates? Timing depends on your wedding type: Local weddings: 6 to 8 months before the wedding date. Destination weddings: 9 to 12 months in advance, giving guests extra time to book flights, accommodations, and passports. Holiday weekend weddings: 9 to 12 months out — holiday travel fills up fast and guests need lead time to adjust plans. If your wedding is less than 4 months away, skip the save the date and send formal invitations directly. Sending save the dates too early (more than 12 months out) risks guests forgetting or details changing before the wedding. How to Choose the Perfect Save the Date Design Your save the date is the first impression of your wedding. Here is how to pick the right one: Match your wedding style. A rustic barn wedding calls for earthy tones and botanical prints. A black-tie city wedding pairs with foil-pressed or minimalist designs. Consider your color palette. If you have already chosen wedding colors, carry them into your save the date for a cohesive look from the first touchpoint. Photo or no photo. Engagement photos make save the dates feel personal. No-photo designs work well if you prefer a cleaner aesthetic or do not have professional photos yet. Paper or digital. Paper save the dates are keepsakes. Digital save the dates are instant, eco-friendly, and free — ideal for tight timelines or budget-conscious couples. Think about your stationery suite. Joy’s save the date designs coordinate with matching invitations, wedding websites, and thank-you cards, so your entire wedding suite feels unified. Below are ideas for every popular style, with design tips and direct links to matching collections. Think Gatsby-era opulence: chevron borders, sunburst motifs, and gold or silver foil on dark backgrounds. Best for: Glamorous ballroom weddings, roaring twenties themes, New Year’s Eve celebrations, and urban venues with architectural detail. Best for: Seaside ceremonies, destination beach weddings, tropical resort celebrations, and lakeside events. Who it suits: Couples planning a laid-back celebration near the water who want their stationery to reflect the setting. Design tips: Watercolor washes in ocean blues and sunset corals create an effortlessly beachy feel. Add a photo from a beach engagement session to make it personal. Browse Beach Save the Dates on Joy → Black and White Save the Date Ideas Black and white save the dates are timeless, sophisticated, and universally elegant. High-contrast typography, monochrome photography, and clean layouts make a bold statement without relying on color. Best for: Modern weddings, formal affairs, black-tie events, and couples who want a classic look that never feels dated. Who it suits: Couples who appreciate simplicity and want their stationery to feel polished and editorial. Design tips: A black-and-white engagement photo paired with clean sans-serif typography creates a magazine-quality save the date. Add a pop of gold foil for subtle warmth. Browse Black & White Save the Dates on Joy → Bold Save the Date Ideas Bold save the dates use oversized typography, saturated colors, graphic patterns, and unexpected layouts to make an immediate visual impact. These designs demand attention and set the expectation for an energetic celebration. Best for: Modern weddings, festival-style celebrations, colorful receptions, and couples with big personalities. Who it suits: Couples who want to break from tradition and make a statement from the very first announcement. Design tips: Do not be afraid of color. Pair a bold palette (fuchsia and orange, cobalt and chartreuse) with strong typography. Let the design do the talking — keep wording minimal. Browse Bold Save the Dates on Joy → Botanical Save the Date Ideas Botanical save the dates feature illustrated greenery, leaves, ferns, eucalyptus branches, and nature-inspired motifs. The aesthetic is organic and refined — more garden illustration than wild bouquet. Best for: Garden weddings, outdoor ceremonies, greenhouse venues, and nature-inspired celebrations. Who it suits: Couples who love the outdoors and want their stationery to reflect a connection to nature without being rustic. Design tips: Green and white is the classic botanical palette, but adding dusty rose or sage elevates the look. Watercolor botanical illustrations feel more organic than graphic prints. Browse Botanical Save the Dates on Joy → Bright Save the Date Ideas Bright save the dates use vibrant, saturated color palettes — think hot pink, sunshine yellow, electric blue, and tangerine. These designs are joyful, energetic, and impossible to overlook in a stack of mail. Best for: Summer weddings, tropical celebrations, fiesta-themed events, and any wedding that embraces color. Who it suits: Fun-loving couples who want their stationery to reflect their upbeat personality and set an exciting tone. Design tips: Balance bright colors with white space so the design feels intentional rather than overwhelming. A bright border around a clean white center is a strong approach. Browse Bright Save the Dates on Joy → Classic Save the Date Ideas Classic save the dates rely on traditional typography, balanced layouts, and timeless design elements — script fonts, simple borders, and formal wording. These designs never go out of style. Best for: Traditional church weddings, ballroom receptions, country club events, and couples who value timeless elegance over trends. Who it suits: Couples who want their stationery to feel refined, proper, and effortlessly elegant. Design tips: Let the typography carry the design. A beautiful script font on quality card stock needs very little embellishment. Ivory, cream, and navy are classic base colors. Browse Classic Save the Dates on Joy → Elegant Save the Date Ideas Elegant save the dates exude sophistication through refined typography, luxurious finishes, and restrained color palettes. Foil accents, letterpress textures, and calligraphy-style fonts define this category. Best for: Black-tie weddings, formal evening celebrations, luxury hotel venues, and estate weddings. Who it suits: Couples planning an upscale affair who want every detail — starting with the save the date — to feel polished and premium. Design tips: Gold or rose gold foil on thick card stock instantly elevates any design. Keep the layout clean and let the materials speak for themselves. Browse Elegant Save the Dates on Joy → Floral Save the Date Ideas Floral save the dates range from delicate watercolor blooms to bold, graphic flower prints. This is one of the most popular and versatile save the date styles — there is a floral design for every season and wedding aesthetic. Best for: Spring and summer weddings, garden parties, romantic celebrations, and any wedding with flowers as a key design element. Who it suits: Couples who love romance, nature, and want a feminine or garden-inspired feel. Design tips: Match the floral style to your wedding florals. Soft watercolor blooms for a romantic garden wedding. Bold, graphic florals for a modern celebration. Dried flower motifs for a boho or rustic aesthetic. Browse Floral Save the Dates on Joy → Minimalist Save the Date Ideas Minimalist save the dates strip away decoration and rely on clean typography, generous white space, and simple layouts. Every element is intentional — nothing extra, nothing missing. Best for: Modern weddings, loft and gallery venues, intimate celebrations, and couples who believe less is more. Who it suits: Design-conscious couples who appreciate restraint and want their save the date to feel sleek and contemporary. Design tips: Choose one strong typeface and let it anchor the design. A single-color palette (black on white, gray on cream) keeps things sophisticated. If adding a photo, use a single image with plenty of breathing room. Browse Minimalist Save the Dates on Joy → Modern Save the Date Ideas Modern save the dates push boundaries with asymmetric layouts, contemporary typography, unexpected color combinations, and graphic design elements. They feel fresh, current, and design-forward. Best for: Urban weddings, rooftop celebrations, art gallery venues, and couples with a strong sense of design. Who it suits: Trend-aware couples who want their stationery to feel like it belongs in a design magazine. Design tips: Experiment with split layouts, color blocking, and mixed typography (pairing a serif with a sans-serif). Modern does not mean cold — warm tones and playful touches keep it inviting. Browse Modern Save the Dates on Joy → Rustic Save the Date Ideas Rustic save the dates draw from natural textures, earth tones, hand-drawn elements, and organic aesthetics. Think kraft paper textures, woodgrain accents, wildflower illustrations, and warm, inviting palettes. Best for: Barn weddings, vineyard celebrations, farm-to-table events, mountain venues, and outdoor ceremonies. Who it suits: Couples who love the warmth of natural materials and want their wedding to feel down-to-earth and welcoming. Design tips: Earth tones (terracotta, olive, burgundy, mustard) paired with hand-lettered fonts create an authentic rustic feel. Wooden magnet save the dates are a popular rustic choice that doubles as a fridge keepsake. Browse Rustic Save the Dates on Joy → Vintage Save the Date Ideas Vintage save the dates draw inspiration from past eras — Victorian ornamental borders, mid-century typography, retro color palettes, and antique-style illustrations. The look is nostalgic without being old-fashioned. Best for: Historic venue weddings, estate celebrations, themed weddings (1920s, 1950s, 1970s), and couples who love antique aesthetics. Who it suits: Couples with a fondness for history, antiques, and design elements that carry a sense of timelessness. Design tips: Sepia tones and aged textures set a vintage mood instantly. Pair with a classic serif font and ornamental details. Vintage filmstrip or postcard formats add extra nostalgia. Browse Vintage Save the Dates on Joy → Romantic Save the Date Ideas Romantic save the dates are soft, dreamy, and heartfelt — flowing calligraphy, blush and rose tones, watercolor washes, and delicate details that evoke love and tenderness. Best for: Garden weddings, candlelit evening celebrations, chateau and estate venues, and Valentine’s Day or spring weddings. Who it suits: Sentimental couples who want their stationery to feel like a love letter. Design tips: Soft pink, lavender, and champagne tones create a romantic palette. Calligraphy script conveys intimacy. A dreamy engagement photo with a soft edit completes the look. Browse Romantic Save the Dates on Joy → Save the Date Ideas by Color Color sets the mood before guests read a single word. Whether you are matching your wedding palette or choosing something that catches the eye, here are save the date ideas organized by color. Beige Save the Dates Beige and neutral-toned save the dates feel warm, organic, and understated. They pair beautifully with earth-toned wedding palettes and natural venues. Ideal for fall weddings, boho celebrations, and couples who want a soft, approachable aesthetic. Beige works well as a background for gold foil text or dark typography. Browse Beige Save the Dates → Black Save the Dates Black save the dates are dramatic, sophisticated, and undeniably bold. A black background with white or metallic text creates a striking contrast that commands attention. Best for formal evening weddings, New Year’s Eve celebrations, and modern black-tie events. Gold or silver foil on black card stock is a particularly luxurious combination. Browse Black Save the Dates → Blue Save the Dates Blue is one of the most versatile wedding colors — from pale dusty blue for romantic celebrations to deep navy for formal affairs to bright cobalt for modern weddings. Blue save the dates feel calm, elegant, and universally appealing. Navy and gold is a classic pairing for traditional weddings, while dusty blue and white creates a soft, romantic feel. Browse Blue Save the Dates → Brown Save the Dates Brown and chocolate-toned save the dates feel earthy, warm, and grounded. They evoke natural materials like wood, leather, and kraft paper. Best for rustic weddings, autumn celebrations, and vineyard or farm venues. Pair brown tones with cream text and botanical illustrations for a coherent earthy aesthetic. Browse Brown Save the Dates → Gold Save the Dates Gold save the dates radiate luxury and celebration. Whether achieved through foil stamping, metallic ink, or printed gold tones, they signal a special occasion. Gold is the universal color of elegance and works for formal weddings, holiday celebrations, and glamorous events. Pair with white, black, or deep jewel tones. Browse Gold Save the Dates → Gray Save the Dates Gray save the dates are refined, modern, and surprisingly versatile. From pale silver-gray for a soft, romantic look to charcoal for contemporary sophistication, gray serves as an elegant neutral. Best for modern weddings, winter celebrations, and industrial-chic venues. Pairs beautifully with blush, white, or greenery accents. Browse Gray Save the Dates → Green Save the Dates Green save the dates range from deep emerald for formal weddings to sage and olive for organic, natural aesthetics. Green evokes nature, growth, and freshness. Best for garden weddings, outdoor celebrations, and botanical-themed events. Sage green with white calligraphy is a popular combination for its earthy elegance. Browse Green Save the Dates → Pink Save the Dates Pink save the dates cover a wide spectrum — from soft blush and dusty rose for romantic celebrations to hot pink and fuchsia for bold, modern weddings. Pink is inherently romantic and celebratory. Best for spring and summer weddings, garden parties, and couples who embrace a feminine aesthetic. Blush and gold is an enduringly popular pairing. Browse Pink Save the Dates → Purple Save the Dates Purple save the dates bring richness and depth — from soft lavender for a dreamy, romantic feel to deep plum and aubergine for dramatic elegance. Purple is historically associated with royalty and luxury. Best for formal weddings, vineyard celebrations, and fall or winter events. Lavender and silver is a refined combination, while plum and gold feels regal. Browse Purple Save the Dates → Red Save the Dates Red save the dates are passionate, festive, and impossible to miss. From deep burgundy for autumn elegance to bright red for holiday weddings, red makes a powerful statement. Best for winter weddings, Valentine’s Day celebrations, Chinese-inspired wedding aesthetics, and couples who want boldness from the start. Burgundy and gold is a timeless fall pairing. A white base lets typography, photography, and subtle design elements take center stage. Best for any wedding style — white works as a canvas for every aesthetic, from minimalist to ornate. White with gold foil is timeless. White with black typography is modern and crisp. Browse White Save the Dates → Yellow Save the Dates Yellow save the dates are cheerful, sunny, and full of warmth. From soft butter tones to vibrant sunflower shades, yellow signals joy and celebration. Best for spring and summer weddings, outdoor garden parties, and couples who want their stationery to feel happy and welcoming. Pair yellow with white, gray, or navy for balance. Paper Save the Dates Paper save the dates are physical keepsakes that guests can hold, display, and stick on their refrigerators. There is a tangible quality to receiving a beautifully printed card in the mail that digital cannot replicate. Premium feel. Thick card stock, foil stamping, letterpress textures, and specialty finishes (vellum overlays, wax seals) create a luxury impression before guests even read the words. Keepsake value. Many guests save physical save the dates as mementos — especially magnets, which stay on the fridge as a daily reminder of your celebration. Best for: Traditional and formal weddings, couples who value tactile quality, and weddings where the stationery is part of the design narrative. Joy’s paper save the dates are part of a coordinated stationery suite — your save the date, invitation, wedding website, and thank-you cards all share a unified design. A zero-waste option that still looks beautiful. Budget-friendly. Many digital save the date designs on Joy are free, making them ideal for couples allocating their budget elsewhere. Easy sharing. Guests can forward the save the date, add the date directly to their digital calendar, and click through to your wedding website — all from their phone. Digital save the dates are not a lesser option — they are a modern, practical choice that works especially well for casual weddings, destination weddings where guests are spread across time zones, and couples who want to keep things simple. Browse Digital Save the Dates on Joy → Save the Date Ideas by Price Free Digital Save the Dates Joy offers a collection of free digital save the date designs that you can customize with your names, date, and photo, then send directly to your guest list at no cost. Free does not mean generic — these designs are professionally crafted and fully customizable. Free digital save the dates are ideal for couples who want to save their budget for the wedding itself or who are planning a casual celebration where a formal printed card is not necessary. Premium Paper and Digital Save the Dates Premium save the dates — both paper and upgraded digital designs — include specialty finishes like foil stamping, letterpress, vellum overlays, and premium card stock. These are designed for couples who want their first wedding communication to make a strong impression. Paper save the dates are priced per card and include envelopes. Premium digital designs offer elevated aesthetics with optional add-ons like matching envelope liners and custom monograms. Browse Save the Dates by Price on Joy → Save the Date Ideas by Photo Photo Save the Dates Photo save the dates feature your engagement photos (or any photos that capture your relationship) as the centerpiece of the design. This is the most personal format — guests see your faces alongside the date and immediately connect the announcement to you as a couple. Best for: Couples who have professional engagement photos and want to showcase them, or couples who want a personal, warm feel. Design tips: Choose a photo with good lighting and a clear background. Full-bleed photo designs create maximum impact. If using multiple photos, a collage or filmstrip layout gives variety without clutter. Browse Photo Save the Dates on Joy → No-Photo Save the Dates No-photo save the dates rely entirely on typography, illustration, color, and design elements to make an impression. They are clean, versatile, and do not require a photo shoot. Best for: Couples who have not done an engagement shoot yet, prefer a design-forward aesthetic, or simply like the look of illustration-only stationery. Design tips: Without a photo to anchor the design, typography and layout become even more important. Choose a strong typeface and let the design style (floral, minimalist, art deco) carry the visual weight. Browse No-Photo Save the Dates on Joy → Save the Date Ideas by Foil Foil stamping adds a metallic sheen to text, borders, or design elements — catching the light and adding a tactile, luxurious dimension that flat printing cannot achieve. Gold Foil Save the Dates Gold foil is the most popular foil option for save the dates. It adds warmth, elegance, and a classic luxury feel. Gold foil pairs naturally with white, ivory, black, navy, and blush backgrounds. It works for everything from traditional formal weddings to modern celebrations with a touch of glamour. Browse Gold Foil Save the Dates on Joy → Save the Date Ideas by Orientation Portrait Save the Dates Portrait-oriented (vertical) save the dates are the traditional layout. They work well for designs that stack text vertically (names, date, location in a column), showcase a single vertical photo, or replicate the proportions of a formal invitation. Best for: Classic and formal designs, single-photo layouts, and save the dates that will be displayed on refrigerators or bulletin boards. Design tips: Portrait orientation naturally draws the eye from top to bottom, making it ideal for hierarchical information: names at the top, date in the middle, location at the bottom. Browse Portrait Save the Dates on Joy → Landscape Save the Dates Landscape-oriented (horizontal) save the dates offer a wider canvas that works well for panoramic photos, side-by-side layouts, and designs with more horizontal visual elements. Best for: Postcard-style designs, wide engagement photos (scenic backgrounds, panoramic landscapes), and save the dates with a lot of visual content. Design tips: A landscape orientation feels more casual and modern. Use the extra horizontal space for a panoramic photo on one side and text on the other, or split the design into two balanced halves. Browse Landscape Save the Dates on Joy → When to Send Save the Dates: A Complete Timeline Getting the timing right ensures guests have enough notice without sending so early that your save the date gets lost or forgotten. Local Weddings Send save the dates 6 to 8 months before the wedding. Most guests will be driving or taking a short flight, so they need enough time to request days off and arrange accommodations, but not so much that the date feels distant. Destination Weddings Send save the dates 9 to 12 months in advance. Guests need extra time to book international or domestic flights, apply for passports or visas, arrange extended time off, and budget for travel expenses. The earlier notice also helps them take advantage of lower airfares. Holiday Weekend Weddings Send save the dates 9 to 12 months out. Holiday weekends (Memorial Day, Labor Day, Fourth of July, Thanksgiving weekend) are popular travel times, and guests may already have competing plans. Early notice helps them prioritize your celebration. Save the Date Timeline Checklist 12 months out: Finalize your wedding date and venue. Begin designing save the dates for destination or holiday weddings. 9 to 10 months out: Send save the dates for destination and holiday weddings. 6 to 8 months out: Send save the dates for local weddings. 4 to 6 months out: Follow up with formal invitations (whether or not you sent save the dates). Under 4 months: Skip the save the date and send formal invitations directly. Include your wedding website URL on your save the date so guests can immediately access travel information, hotel recommendations, and RSVP details as you add them. Frequently Asked Questions When should I send save the dates? Send save the dates 6 to 8 months before the wedding for local celebrations, or 9 to 12 months for destination weddings and holiday weekends. If your wedding is less than 4 months away, skip the save the date and go directly to formal invitations. What information should I include on a save the date? Include both partners’ names, the wedding date, the city or general location (a full address is not necessary yet), a note that a formal invitation will follow, and your wedding website URL. Do not include registry information on save the dates — save that for the invitation and wedding website. Do save the dates require an RSVP? No. Save the dates are informational — they ask guests to hold the date, not to formally respond. The RSVP comes later with the formal invitation, typically 2 to 3 months before the wedding. Joy’s online RSVP system makes it easy to collect responses when the time comes. Should I include my wedding website URL on the save the date? Yes. Your wedding website is where guests go for travel details, hotel recommendations, registry links, and event information. Including the URL on the save the date gives guests a place to find answers immediately, and you can update the website as details are finalized. Can I send digital save the dates instead of paper? Absolutely. Digital save the dates are a legitimate, increasingly popular option. They are instant, eco-friendly, budget-friendly, and allow guests to click directly to your wedding website or add the date to their calendar. Joy offers a range of free and premium digital save the date designs . Can I change my wedding date after sending save the dates? Yes, though it requires sending an update to all guests. If you have a wedding website (and you should), update the date there immediately and send a brief email or message to your guest list with the new date. If you sent paper save the dates, a digital update via email is perfectly acceptable for the correction — you do not need to reprint and mail a new card.

title: Dave Wright on Building the Infinite Company
summary: Dave Wright on building a human and AI workforce, where AI expands what your business can create, not just what it does faster.
body_text: The Infinite Company : A Conversation with Dave Wright Share: Share Share Dave Wright is Chief Innovation Officer at ServiceNow, where he helps organizations explore how AI and emerging technologies are reshaping business and work. A technology executive with nearly three decades of experience , Dave has held leadership roles spanning strategy, solutions consulting, cloud infrastructure, and enterprise transformation. He is the author of a new book The Infinite Company , which explores how organizations can combine human ingenuity with AI to become infinitely more powerful. We sat down with Dave to talk about what can be created w hen Human + AI become your new workforce. What do you mean when you talk about an “Infinite Company”? An Infinite Company is designed to become more capable, intelligent, and adaptive over time by combining human ingenuity with AI. Most organizations use AI to make existing work faster and more efficient. Infinite Companies go further. They rethink how work gets done, how decisions are made, and how value is created. The goal is not simply optimization. It is expanding what is possible for the business, its employees, and its customers. If you walked into an organization and knew nothing about it, what would tell you that it was operating as an Infinite Company rather than a conventional one? You would notice it in the conversations. People would not be worried about being replaced by AI. They would talk about it as a tool that helps them think, learn, and create better outcomes. The focus would be less on activities and more on results. People would describe what they achieved, not simply what they did. Most importantly, the organization would be more curious than defensive, constantly asking what could be reinvented rather than simply optimized. You have said workflows are becoming more important than functions. What does that actually look like inside a company? Functions are not disappearing, but they matter less than how work flows across the enterprise. Most organizations are still structured around departments, while value is created through workflows that cross multiple teams, systems, and functions. As AI becomes more embedded in work, leaders need to understand how decisions move, where bottlenecks exist, and where humans and AI should collaborate. In many cases, workflow design will become more important than organization design. Companies that understand how work flows will have a significant advantage over those that simply automate individual tasks. An infinite company is designed to become more capable, intelligent, and adaptive over time by combining human ingenuity with AI. What are the first signs that an organization’s operating model is starting to change because of AI? The first sign is that people begin focusing on outcomes rather than activities. Work starts being measured by what was accomplished rather than how many steps were completed. You also begin to see management structures flatten. Traditional managers spend a great deal of time coordinating work. As AI takes on more of that coordination, leaders can focus more on decision-making, coaching, and handling exceptions. The organization becomes faster, more connected, and less dependent on hierarchy. What organizational changes should leaders be making right now? Start with workflows, not technology. Choose a workflow that matters to the business and redesign it from end to end. Don’t begin by asking where AI can be inserted. Begin by asking whether the workflow itself should be redesigned. Leaders should also establish clear ownership for critical workflows and measure business outcomes rather than AI adoption. The companies making the most progress are not running dozens of disconnected pilots. They are fundamentally rethinking how work gets done. What jobs or roles do you think will look fundamentally different five years from now? Many roles will spend less time gathering information and more time applying judgment. Managers will spend less time coordinating work and more time leading teams that include both people and AI agents. We’re also likely to see new roles emerge around workflow design, AI orchestration, governance, and oversight. Organizations will need people who understand not only how AI works, but how humans and AI work together to create value. In many cases, workflow design will become more important than organization design. What is the biggest risk leaders should be paying attention to right now that isn’t getting enough attention? The biggest risk is deploying AI without truly understanding it. Many organizations are making significant investments based on pilot results, vendor presentations, and market momentum without fully understanding where AI succeeds, where it fails, and what outcomes it is producing. At the same time, leaders must be careful not to outsource too much thinking. AI should strengthen human judgment, not replace it. Organizations still need people who can challenge assumptions, ask difficult questions, and make decisions when the answer is not obvious. If you were advising a leadership team preparing for the next five years, what is the one mindset shift you would want them to make today? Stop asking how AI can make the current business more efficient and start asking what becomes possible because AI exists. Most leadership teams have been trained to optimize what already exists. The next generation of leaders will use AI to rethink products, services, customer experiences, and entirely new business models. The organizations that win will not necessarily be the ones that deploy the most AI. They will be the ones that use AI to create something they could not have created before.
